issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: The snake-related trigger is hard to link coherently to the rest of this sexual-assault profile. Other triggers and strategies center on emergency/police/location cues, while no threat, appraisal, or memory content connects to animals or snakes. This makes that item look clinically disconnected rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Compulsive Cleaning: I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
issues.explanation: Compulsive cleaning can occur after sexual assault, but in this profile it is not supported by the other selected items or the formulation. The active pattern strongly links triggers, threat, and negative appraisals to maladaptive strategies, yet the listed triggers/threats/appraisals point to hypervigilance, emergency/uniform cues, and situational avoidance rather than contamination, dirtiness, or washing/control themes. As selected here, the cleaning item appears insufficiently connected to the rest of the profile.

vignette:
Khalil was 54 when he finally spoke in detail about the assault that had happened years earlier, and even then he did so in a careful, measured way, as if staying precise might keep the memory contained. He was a software engineer, single, and lived alone in a small apartment not far from his office. By the time he came for help, he had built his days around predictability: the same routes, the same coffee shop, the same desk in a quiet part of the open-plan office, the same few places in the city where he felt he could relax enough to breathe. He said there were only a very limited number of places that still felt safe, and that small circle had narrowed over time.

The assault had taken place after a work-related evening years before, when he was unexpectedly alone with a man in a position of authority. Khalil described how the other man's status had made the situation feel impossible to challenge in the moment, and how quickly the interaction turned from uneasy to terrifying. He did not give details easily, but what stayed with him most was the humiliation and the sense that he had been trapped by someone who should have been trustworthy. In the months afterward, he kept returning to one thought: what happened to him was deeply unfair, and nothing had been done about it. He said that belief sat beside another that he could not quite shake, that the event happened because of the way he acted, because he had not left sooner, had not spoken up, had not seen it coming. He knew these thoughts did not fit neatly together, but they both remained vivid to him.

Over time, Khalil began organizing his life around avoiding anything that brought back the atmosphere of that night. He went out of his way to avoid the building and nearby streets where the assault had occurred, and he adjusted his commuting route so he would not pass the place even by accident. He became intensely uneasy around military or police uniforms and around weapons, and he would cross the street or turn away in stores if he saw a man in uniform near the entrance. He found it especially hard to be around people in authority or uniform, not because he believed every one of them was dangerous, but because the sight of them pulled him back into the same helplessness. At work, this meant he avoided the conference floor when external security or visiting officials were present, and he had quietly declined chances to attend certain client sites. His colleagues saw him as private and dependable, but they did not know how much effort it took for him to keep his face steady when he spotted a uniform in the lobby.

Certain sounds hit him before he had time to think. Sirens, especially ambulances, brought on an immediate jolt, and he would feel himself tense and scan the street or office windows as if something urgent were unfolding nearby. He described reacting as though he were in danger even when nothing was actually wrong, and this was most obvious in public places where an ambulance or emergency vehicle passed and his body seemed to decide before his mind did. In those moments he would search for exits, watch other people's faces, and look repeatedly over his shoulder. He said he constantly scanned his surroundings for signs of danger, checking who was near him, where they were standing, and whether any man was getting too close. Being alone with men, especially in enclosed spaces like elevators, stairwells, or empty corridors, remained particularly difficult. He would choose a longer route rather than share a small space if he could avoid it, and he had arranged his schedule at the office so he was less likely to be alone after hours.

Khalil said the changes became more noticeable to others through the small accommodations that accumulated. He stopped staying late with coworkers, even when deadlines made it awkward. He turned down invitations that involved crowded events with security at the entrance. He became increasingly selective about where he would meet friends, insisting on familiar restaurants and sitting with his back to a wall. He did not describe panic in dramatic terms; instead, he spoke of vigilance, of being on guard, of never fully relaxing. He was tired of living this way, but he also feared that if he let his guard drop, something would happen again. What disturbed him most was that he no longer trusted even ordinary moments to stay ordinary.

He came for help after a recent evening when an ambulance siren sounded near his apartment and he found himself standing frozen by the window, heart racing, watching the street below as if expecting the worst. That moment left him ashamed and exhausted. He said he was tired of feeling cut off from normal life and frightened by the thought that he would never be able to feel normal emotions again. At the same time, he was still carrying the belief that no one had done anything about what happened to him, and he wanted a place where he could say that aloud without being dismissed. By the time he sat down in the consulting room, Khalil was hoping for relief from the constant scanning, from the sudden false alarms, and from the shrinking map of places where he felt safe, even as he remained most afraid that the assault had permanently altered the way he would experience the world and himself.
